items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "standard deviation"?
options: A statistical test used to find whether the difference between the means of two samples of continuous data is significant.
An estimate of how close a sample mean is likely to be to the true population mean (SM = s ÷ √n).
Variation in which a characteristic has a range of values between two extremes, such as height, usually controlled by many genes and influenced by the environment.
A measure of the spread of data about the mean; about 68% of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean in a normal distribution.
items.answer: A measure of the spread of data about the mean; about 68% of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean in a normal distribution.
items.markingKey: Standard deviation: a measure of the spread of data about the mean; about 68% of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean in a normal distribution.

items.stem: Explain why characteristics controlled by several genes show continuous variation.
items.answer: Each gene has alleles that add a small amount to the phenotype (additive effect); many combinations of alleles give a range of phenotypes; the environment adds further variation.
items.markingKey: many genes, additive [1]; many combinations / range [1]; environment [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain how genotype and environment both contribute to the variation in the height of a crop plant.
items.answer: Genotype sets the potential height through alleles of many genes; environmental factors (light, water, minerals, temperature) determine how far that potential is reached; phenotype results from the interaction.
items.markingKey: genetic potential [1]; environmental factors [1]; interaction [1] [3]

items.stem: Aisha measured the wing length of house sparrows from a rural area (sample A, n = 15) and house sparrows from a city (sample B, n = 8). Sample A: mean 76.2 mm, standard deviation 1.32. Sample B: mean 72.75, standard deviation 1.909. Explain why a t-test, rather than a chi-squared test, is appropriate for these data.
items.answer: The data are continuous measurements (approximately normally distributed) and two means are being compared; χ² is for counts in categories.
items.markingKey: The data are continuous measurements (approximately normally distributed) and two means are being compared [1]; χ² is for counts in categories [1] [2]

items.stem: Ana measured the wing length of house sparrows from a rural area (sample A, n = 8) and house sparrows from a city (sample B, n = 8). Sample A: mean 76.12 mm, standard deviation 1.553. Sample B: mean 74.75, standard deviation 1.832. (a) State a null hypothesis for this investigation. (b) Explain why a t-test, rather than a chi-squared test, is appropriate for these data.
items.answer: (a) There is no significant difference between the mean wing length of the two samples. (b) The data are continuous measurements (approximately normally distributed) and two means are being compared; χ² is for counts in categories.
items.markingKey: (a) There is no significant difference between the mean wing length of the two samples [1] (b) The data are continuous measurements (approximately normally distributed) and two means are being compared [1]; χ² is for counts in categories [1] [2]

items.stem: Sofia measured the height or mass of individuals in a herd of goats in Istanbul and found that the data formed a normal distribution. (a) Suggest why individuals of the clone still show variation. (b) Explain the difference between variation caused by genes and variation caused by the environment in terms of whether it can be inherited.
items.answer: (a) Both genetic and environmental differences contribute; e.g. different alleles and different access to food. (b) Genetic variation is passed to offspring in gametes; environmental variation is not inherited (it changes the phenotype, not the alleles).
items.markingKey: (a) Both genetic and environmental differences contribute [1]; e.g. different alleles and different access to food [1] [2] (b) Genetic variation is passed to offspring in gametes [1]; environmental variation is not inherited (it changes the phenotype, not the alleles) [1] [2]

items.stem: Which characteristic shows continuous variation?
options: Presence or absence of horns in cattle
Leaf length in a population of oak trees
items.answer: Leaf length in a population of oak trees
items.markingKey: Range of values, polygenic.

items.stem: Explain why a t-test is more reliable than simply comparing two means.
items.answer: Means differ by chance; the t-test takes into account the spread (standard deviation) and sample size, giving the probability that the difference is due to chance.
items.markingKey: chance variation [1]; uses spread and sample size [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the standard deviation is a useful statistic when describing continuous data.
items.answer: It shows the spread/variability of data around the mean; a small SD means values are close to the mean; it allows comparison of variation between samples.
items.markingKey: spread around mean [1]; comparison / reliability [1] [2]

items.stem: The values for the number of seeds per pod in a sample of bean pods were 16, 26, 30, 34, 36, 39. Calculate the mean and the standard deviation, using s = √(Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1)).
Compare continuous and discontinuous variation and explain how genes and the environment contribute to each.
items.answer: Discontinuous: categories, one/few genes, alleles with large effects, dominance/codominance, little environment (e.g. blood group). Continuous: range, polygenes with additive small effects, environment (height, mass), normal distribution; phenotype = genotype + environment; t-test for comparison.
items.markingKey: definitions [2]; genetic basis of each [2]; environmental influence [1]; examples [1]; statistical treatment [1] [7]

items.stem: Freya measured the height or mass of individuals in a clone of strawberry plants in Santiago and found that the data formed a normal distribution. (a) Explain why the data form a normal distribution. (b) Describe how you would decide whether the mean value differs significantly from that of a second population.
items.answer: (a) The characteristic shows continuous variation: it is controlled by many genes (polygenes) with additive effects, plus environmental effects; most individuals are near the mean with few at the extremes. (b) Measure a large random sample from each; calculate means and standard deviations; carry out a t-test with df = n₁ + n₂ − 2; compare t with the critical value at p = 0.05.
items.markingKey: (a) polygenic [1]; additive / environment [1]; most near mean [1] [3] (b) random samples [1]; t-test [1]; compare with critical value [1] [3]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "natural selection"?
options: The process by which individuals with alleles that give an advantage in a particular environment are more likely to survive and reproduce, so the allele frequency increases.
An environmental factor, such as predation or disease, that affects the chances of survival and reproduction of individuals.
Selection that favours one extreme phenotype, shifting the mean (e.g. antibiotic resistance).
Selection that favours intermediate phenotypes and acts against extremes, reducing variation (e.g. human birth mass).
items.answer: The process by which individuals with alleles that give an advantage in a particular environment are more likely to survive and reproduce, so the allele frequency increases.
items.markingKey: Natural selection: the process by which individuals with alleles that give an advantage in a particular environment are more likely to survive and reproduce, so the allele frequency increases.

items.stem: Explain how antibiotic resistance spreads in a population of bacteria.
items.answer: Random mutation produces an allele for resistance; antibiotic is the selection pressure; non-resistant bacteria are killed; resistant bacteria survive and reproduce, passing the allele on (vertically, or by plasmid transfer); frequency of the allele increases (directional selection).
items.markingKey: mutation [1]; selection pressure [1]; survival and reproduction of resistant [1]; allele frequency increases [1] [4]

items.stem: Explain how the sickle cell allele is maintained at a high frequency in regions with malaria.
items.answer: Heterozygotes (sickle cell trait) are more resistant to malaria and do not have severe anaemia; they survive and reproduce more than either homozygote; so both alleles are kept in the population (heterozygote advantage).
items.markingKey: heterozygote resistant to malaria [1]; HbˢHbˢ anaemia / HbᴬHbᴬ malaria [1]; both alleles maintained [1] [3]

items.stem: Omar is studying a recessive dark wing colour among moths in a city park. About 1 in 50 moths show the condition, which is caused by a homozygous recessive genotype. Calculate the percentage of the population who are heterozygous carriers.

Amara is studying albinism among people in a small island population. About 1 in 400 people show the condition, which is caused by a homozygous recessive genotype. (a) Calculate the frequency of the recessive allele, q. (b) Calculate the frequency of the dominant allele, p.

Tomás is studying a recessive white-flowered allele among plants in a meadow. About 1 in 10,000 plants show the condition, which is caused by a homozygous recessive genotype. (a) Calculate the frequency of the recessive allele, q. (b) Calculate the percentage of the population who are heterozygous carriers.

A population of 20 lizards was carried to a new island in Istanbul's region by a storm. After 30 generations, the frequency of an allele for striped skin was 0.8, compared with 0.3 on the mainland. (a) Explain how the founder effect could account for this difference. (b) State why the Hardy–Weinberg principle would not apply to the island population.
items.answer: (a) The founders were a small, random sample of the mainland population, which by chance had a high frequency of the striped allele; the new population started with different allele frequencies and less genetic variation. (b) The population is small (drift) and there may be selection, so allele frequencies are not constant.
items.markingKey: (a) small sample [1]; by chance not representative [1]; reduced variation [1] [3] (b) The population is small (drift) and there may be selection, so allele frequencies are not constant [1]

items.stem: A population of 12 lizards was carried to a new island in Muscat's region by a storm. After 30 generations, the frequency of an allele for striped skin was 0.73, compared with 0.26 on the mainland. (a) Explain how the founder effect could account for this difference. (b) Suggest how natural selection could also explain the high frequency of the striped allele.
items.answer: (a) The founders were a small, random sample of the mainland population, which by chance had a high frequency of the striped allele; the new population started with different allele frequencies and less genetic variation. (b) If striped skin gives better camouflage on the island, striped lizards survive and reproduce more, increasing the allele frequency (directional selection).
items.markingKey: (a) small sample [1]; by chance not representative [1]; reduced variation [1] [3] (b) selective advantage [1]; survival and reproduction / allele frequency [1] [2]

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "selection that favours both extremes and acts against intermediates, possibly leading to two forms"?
items.answer: Disruptive selection
items.markingKey: Disruptive selection: selection that favours both extremes and acts against intermediates, possibly leading to two forms.

items.stem: Which type of selection is shown when the mean birth mass of human babies stays constant over many generations?
items.answer: Stabilising
items.markingKey: Very small and very large babies have lower survival.

items.stem: Explain the difference between natural selection and genetic drift.
items.answer: Selection changes allele frequencies non-randomly because some alleles increase fitness; drift changes allele frequencies randomly by chance, especially in small populations, regardless of advantage.
items.markingKey: selection non-random / advantage [1]; drift random / chance [1]; small populations [1] [3]

items.stem: In a population of salmon, large males fight for females and very small males sneak matings, while medium-sized males rarely reproduce. Identify the type of selection and explain how it changes the population.
items.answer: Disruptive selection: both extremes reproduce more than intermediates, so alleles for both extremes are favoured.
items.markingKey: type [1]; explanation in terms of survival, reproduction and allele frequency [2] [3]

items.stem: Ines is studying cystic fibrosis among people of European descent. About 1 in 25 people show the condition, which is caused by a homozygous recessive genotype. Calculate the percentage of the population who are heterozygous carriers.

A population of 50 lizards was carried to a new island in Mumbai's region by a storm. After 30 generations, the frequency of an allele for striped skin was 0.75, compared with 0.24 on the mainland. (a) Suggest how natural selection could also explain the high frequency of the striped allele. (b) State why the Hardy–Weinberg principle would not apply to the island population.
items.answer: (a) If striped skin gives better camouflage on the island, striped lizards survive and reproduce more, increasing the allele frequency (directional selection). (b) The population is small (drift) and there may be selection, so allele frequencies are not constant.
items.markingKey: (a) selective advantage [1]; survival and reproduction / allele frequency [1] [2] (b) The population is small (drift) and there may be selection, so allele frequencies are not constant [1]

items.stem: Explain how natural selection can change allele frequencies in a population, with reference to stabilising, directional and disruptive selection.
items.answer: Variation by mutation and meiosis; overproduction; competition; selection pressures; individuals with advantageous alleles survive and reproduce, pass on alleles; stabilising favours intermediates (birth mass); directional shifts mean (antibiotic resistance); disruptive favours extremes; genetic drift in small populations; Hardy–Weinberg to detect change.
items.markingKey: variation and overproduction [1]; selection and allele frequency [2]; stabilising [1]; directional [1]; disruptive [1]; drift / HW [1] [7]

items.stem: A population of 50 lizards was carried to a new island in Santiago's region by a storm. After 30 generations, the frequency of an allele for striped skin was 0.68, compared with 0.1 on the mainland. (a) Explain how the founder effect could account for this difference. (b) Suggest how natural selection could also explain the high frequency of the striped allele.
items.answer: (a) The founders were a small, random sample of the mainland population, which by chance had a high frequency of the striped allele; the new population started with different allele frequencies and less genetic variation. (b) If striped skin gives better camouflage on the island, striped lizards survive and reproduce more, increasing the allele frequency (directional selection).
items.markingKey: (a) small sample [1]; by chance not representative [1]; reduced variation [1] [3] (b) selective advantage [1]; survival and reproduction / allele frequency [1] [2]

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "the reduced vigour and fertility of offspring from closely related parents, caused by increased homozygosity of harmful recessive alleles"?
items.answer: Inbreeding depression
items.markingKey: Inbreeding depression: the reduced vigour and fertility of offspring from closely related parents, caused by increased homozygosity of harmful recessive alleles.

items.stem: Explain how a farmer could use selective breeding to increase milk yield in a herd of dairy cattle.
items.answer: Measure milk yield of cows; choose cows with highest yield; choose bulls whose daughters have high yields (progeny testing); breed using artificial insemination; select the best offspring and repeat over many generations.
items.markingKey: select high-yield cows [1]; progeny-tested bulls [1]; AI / IVF [1]; repeat over generations [1] [4]

items.stem: Explain why inbreeding and hybridisation are both used in the breeding of maize.
items.answer: Inbreeding produces homozygous, uniform lines but with low vigour; crossing two different inbred lines produces heterozygous F1 hybrids with hybrid vigour and uniformity; seed must be produced each year.
items.markingKey: inbred lines uniform but weak [1]; crossing gives hybrid vigour [1]; F1 uniform / new seed yearly [1] [3]

items.stem: Records from a breeding programme in Hanoi show that the mean grain yield of rice rose from 2.2 t ha⁻¹ in 1960 to 6.2 t ha⁻¹ in 2020. Calculate the percentage increase.

Records from a breeding programme in Karachi show that the mean grain yield of rice rose from 2.2 t ha⁻¹ in 1950 to 5.7 t ha⁻¹ in 2010. (a) Calculate the percentage increase. (b) Calculate the mean rate of increase per year.
items.answer: (a) 159% (b) 0.058 t ha⁻¹ per year

items.stem: Plant breeders in Dhaka want to produce a new variety of rice with tolerance of flooding and high yield. (a) Explain why the dwarfing alleles in modern wheat and rice increased yield. (b) Suggest one advantage of genetic engineering compared with selective breeding for this purpose.
items.answer: (a) Short stems (reduced response to or production of gibberellin) resist lodging (falling over) and more photosynthate goes to grain rather than stem. (b) Faster; a single gene can be transferred without unwanted alleles; genes can come from other species.
items.markingKey: (a) reduced gibberellin effect [1]; resist lodging / more to grain [1] [2] (b) Faster; a single gene can be transferred without unwanted alleles; genes can come from other species [1]

items.stem: Why is milk yield in bulls assessed by progeny testing?
options: Bulls do not produce milk, so their daughters' yields are measured
Bulls produce more milk than cows
items.answer: Bulls do not produce milk, so their daughters' yields are measured
items.markingKey: The bull carries alleles for milk yield.

items.stem: Why do breeders cross two different inbred lines of maize?
options: To reduce yield variation in the F2
To produce uniform F1 plants showing hybrid vigour
items.answer: To produce uniform F1 plants showing hybrid vigour
items.markingKey: Heterozygous F1 are vigorous and uniform.

items.stem: Explain how breeders have produced varieties of rice and wheat resistant to fungal diseases.
items.answer: Cross a high-yield variety with a variety (often wild) carrying alleles for resistance; select offspring showing resistance and high yield; backcross and repeat selection over many generations.
items.markingKey: cross with resistant variety [1]; select desired offspring [1]; repeat / backcross [1] [3]

items.stem: The mean annual milk yield of dairy cows in a country rose from 4780 kg in 1970 to 8870 kg in 2020. What was the percentage increase?

Records from a breeding programme in Riyadh show that the mean annual milk yield of dairy cows rose from 4510 kg in 1950 to 8160 kg in 2010. (a) Calculate the mean rate of increase per year. (b) Describe how selective breeding could have contributed to this increase in dairy cows.
items.answer: (a) 61 kg per year (b) Cows with the highest yields bred with progeny-tested bulls by artificial insemination; best offspring selected each generation.
items.markingKey: (a) 3650 ÷ 60 = 61 [1] (b) selection of parents [1]; repeated over generations [1] [2]

items.stem: What is the name for "the possession of more than two complete sets of chromosomes, which can lead to instant sympatric speciation in plants"?
items.answer: Polyploidy
items.markingKey: Polyploidy: the possession of more than two complete sets of chromosomes, which can lead to instant sympatric speciation in plants.

items.stem: Explain how allopatric speciation occurs.
items.answer: A geographical barrier separates a population; no gene flow; different selection pressures, mutations and drift in each; allele frequencies diverge; eventually they cannot interbreed (reproductive isolation) even if reunited.
items.markingKey: barrier / no gene flow [1]; different selection / mutation / drift [1]; allele frequencies change [1]; reproductive isolation [1] [4]

items.stem: Explain how polyploidy can lead to the formation of a new plant species in a single generation.
items.answer: Non-disjunction in meiosis produces diploid gametes; these fuse to form a tetraploid; the tetraploid cannot produce fertile offspring with the diploid parents (triploid offspring are sterile) but can breed with itself.
items.markingKey: diploid gametes [1]; tetraploid [1]; triploid hybrids sterile / reproductive isolation [1] [3]

items.stem: Part of the DNA sequence of a gene in species A is CCCACTCGAACCTGATAACGC. The same region in three other species is: species B: CGCACTCGAACCTGATTACGA; species C: CCCTCTCGCACCTCATACCGC; species D: CCTAGGGGAACCTTCTAACTC. Count the number of base differences between species A and each of the other species.
items.answer: species B: 3, species C: 4, species D: 7
items.markingKey: all three correct [2]

items.stem: Part of the DNA sequence of a gene in the grey wolf is CATGGTATCTTTGTGCGT. The same region in three other species is: the coyote: CATGCTACCTTTGTACGT; the red fox: CATGATAGCCTTTTGCGT; the domestic dog: AGTTGTATCTCTTTGGGG. (a) Use your answers to state which species is most closely related to the grey wolf. Explain your answer. (b) Calculate the percentage difference between the grey wolf and the domestic dog.
items.answer: (a) The coyote: fewest differences, so most recent common ancestor (mutations have had least time to accumulate). (b) 38.9%
items.markingKey: (a) correct species [1]; fewest differences → recent common ancestor [1] [2] (b) 7 ÷ 18 × 100 = 38.9% [1]

items.stem: Two populations of a ground beetle on either side of a mountain range near Bogotá were found to differ in body colour and in the timing of their breeding seasons. When brought together in the laboratory they mated but produced few fertile offspring. (a) Explain how the two populations could have become different. (b) Name the type of isolating mechanism shown by the different breeding seasons.
items.answer: (a) The mountains are a geographical barrier preventing gene flow; different selection pressures (climate, predators) on each side; different mutations and genetic drift; allele frequencies diverged. (b) Temporal (seasonal) isolation — a prezygotic mechanism.
items.markingKey: (a) barrier / no gene flow [1]; selection [1]; mutation / drift [1] [3] (b) Temporal (seasonal) isolation — a prezygotic mechanism [1]

items.stem: What usually starts allopatric speciation?
options: A geographical barrier separating two populations
A change in mating behaviour within one area
items.answer: A geographical barrier separating two populations
items.markingKey: e.g. a mountain range or sea.

items.stem: A diploid plant species (2n = 14) and a related species (2n = 18) form a sterile hybrid whose chromosome number doubles. How many chromosomes does the new fertile species have?

Two populations of a frog species were separated when a river changed course, and now have different mating calls and cannot interbreed. Identify the type of speciation and explain how reproductive isolation arose.
items.answer: Allopatric speciation: a geographical barrier (river) separated them; their calls diverged.
items.markingKey: type [1]; isolating mechanism explained [1]; link to no gene flow / divergence [1] [3]

items.stem: Two populations of squirrels became separated when the Grand Canyon formed, and are now different species. Identify the type of speciation and explain how reproductive isolation arose.
items.answer: Allopatric speciation: a geographical barrier stopped gene flow.
items.markingKey: type [1]; isolating mechanism explained [1]; link to no gene flow / divergence [1] [3]

items.stem: Part of the DNA sequence of a gene in the chimpanzee is GAGCAGGGTCCTGCCCCCTCT. The same region in three other species is: the gorilla: GAGCAGCGTCCTCCCCCCTCT; the orangutan: GCGCGCGAACTTGCCCCCCCT; the human: GTGGATGATACGGCCGCCTTT. (a) Count the number of base differences between the chimpanzee and each of the other species. (b) Calculate the percentage difference between the chimpanzee and the human. (c) Assuming one base difference accumulates in this region every 0.5 million years, estimate when the chimpanzee and the gorilla last shared a common ancestor.
items.answer: (a) the gorilla: 2, the orangutan: 7, the human: 8 (b) 38.1% (c) about 1 million years ago
items.markingKey: (a) all three correct [2] (b) 8 ÷ 21 × 100 = 38.1% [1] (c) 2 × 0.5 = 1 million years [1]; (assumes constant rate) [1] [2]

items.stem: Which is an example of discontinuous variation in humans?
items.answer: ABO blood group
items.markingKey: Distinct categories, controlled by one gene.

items.stem: Elena says: "Discontinuous variation is always caused by the environment." Explain whether Elena is correct.
items.answer: Discontinuous variation is usually genetic, controlled by one or a few genes with little environmental influence.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Discontinuous variation is usually genetic, controlled by one or a few genes with little environmental influence. [2]

Sample B: mean 76.2, standard deviation 1.549. Explain why a t-test, rather than a chi-squared test, is appropriate for these data.
items.answer: The data are continuous measurements (approximately normally distributed) and two means are being compared; χ² is for counts in categories.
items.markingKey: The data are continuous measurements (approximately normally distributed) and two means are being compared [1]; χ² is for counts in categories [1] [2]

items.stem: The values for the heights (cm) of six maize seedlings were 15, 17, 25, 26, 27, 28. Calculate the mean and the standard deviation, using s = √(Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1)).

Mei measured the height or mass of individuals in a population of wild rabbits in Hanoi and found that the data formed a normal distribution. (a) Suggest why individuals of the clone still show variation. (b) Describe how you would decide whether the mean value differs significantly from that of a second population.
items.answer: (a) Both genetic and environmental differences contribute; e.g. different alleles and different access to food. (b) Measure a large random sample from each; calculate means and standard deviations; carry out a t-test with df = n₁ + n₂ − 2; compare t with the critical value at p = 0.05.

items.stem: Which statement about the Hardy–Weinberg principle is correct?
options: It applies only to small populations
It predicts the rate of mutation
Allele frequencies stay constant if there is no selection, mutation, migration or drift and mating is random
Allele frequencies always change each generation
items.answer: Allele frequencies stay constant if there is no selection, mutation, migration or drift and mating is random
items.markingKey: Conditions for equilibrium.

items.stem: In a population, 16% show a recessive phenotype. What is the frequency of the dominant allele?
Explain how disruptive selection could lead to two distinct forms in a population.
items.answer: If both extremes are favoured (e.g. two food sources) and intermediates are selected against, individuals with alleles for extreme phenotypes survive and reproduce more; the population becomes bimodal and may split into two.
items.markingKey: extremes favoured [1]; intermediates selected against [1]; bimodal / possible speciation [1] [3]

items.stem: After warfarin was used widely, rats in some cities became resistant to it. Identify the type of selection and explain how it changes the population.
items.answer: Directional selection: rats with the resistance allele survived poisoning and reproduced, so the resistance allele frequency increased.
items.markingKey: type [1]; explanation in terms of survival, reproduction and allele frequency [2] [3]

items.stem: Isla is studying cystic fibrosis among people of European descent. About 1 in 10,000 people show the condition, which is caused by a homozygous recessive genotype. Calculate the frequency of the recessive allele, q.

A population of 30 lizards was carried to a new island in Accra's region by a storm. After 30 generations, the frequency of an allele for striped skin was 0.65, compared with 0.17 on the mainland. (a) Explain how genetic drift could change the allele frequency further on the island. (b) State why the Hardy–Weinberg principle would not apply to the island population.
items.answer: (a) In a small population, random differences in which individuals reproduce change allele frequencies by chance from generation to generation; alleles may be lost or fixed. (b) The population is small (drift) and there may be selection, so allele frequencies are not constant.
items.markingKey: (a) random / chance [1]; small population [1]; loss or fixation [1] [3] (b) The population is small (drift) and there may be selection, so allele frequencies are not constant [1]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "selective breeding"?
options: The reduced vigour and fertility of offspring from closely related parents, caused by increased homozygosity of harmful recessive alleles.
The increased yield, size or resistance of F1 hybrids from crossing two different inbred lines.
The deliberate crossing of chosen parents over many generations to produce organisms with desired traits.
Assessing the breeding value of a bull by measuring the milk yield of his daughters.
items.answer: The deliberate crossing of chosen parents over many generations to produce organisms with desired traits.
items.markingKey: Selective breeding: the deliberate crossing of chosen parents over many generations to produce organisms with desired traits.

items.stem: Explain why selective breeding reduces genetic diversity.
items.answer: Only a few individuals with desired traits are used as parents, so many alleles are lost from the gene pool; offspring become more homozygous.
items.markingKey: few parents [1]; alleles lost / homozygosity [1] [2]

items.stem: Records from a breeding programme in Muscat show that the mean annual milk yield of dairy cows rose from 4340 kg in 1970 to 8100 kg in 2020. Suggest two reasons, other than selective breeding, for the increase.
items.answer: Better nutrition / feed or fertiliser; irrigation; pesticides / veterinary care; improved management and machinery.
items.markingKey: any 2 from: Better nutrition / feed or fertiliser; irrigation; pesticides / veterinary care; improved management and machinery (1 mark each) [2]

items.stem: Records from a breeding programme in Mumbai show that the mean annual milk yield of dairy cows rose from 4440 kg in 1965 to 7920 kg in 2015. (a) Calculate the percentage increase. (b) Calculate the mean rate of increase per year.
items.answer: (a) 78% (b) 70 kg per year

items.stem: Plant breeders in Kathmandu want to produce a new variety of maize with drought tolerance and uniform cobs. (a) Outline how they could use selective breeding to do this. (b) Explain why the dwarfing alleles in modern wheat and rice increased yield.
items.answer: (a) Identify varieties (including wild relatives / landraces) with each trait; cross them; grow offspring and select those with both traits; self or backcross and select over many generations until true-breeding. (b) Short stems (reduced response to or production of gibberellin) resist lodging (falling over) and more photosynthate goes to grain rather than stem.
items.markingKey: (a) sources of alleles [1]; cross [1]; select offspring [1]; repeat over generations [1] [4] (b) reduced gibberellin effect [1]; resist lodging / more to grain [1] [2]

items.stem: Two populations of frogs in the same pond breed at different times of year. What type of isolation is this?
items.answer: Temporal isolation
items.markingKey: Prezygotic.

items.stem: Explain why comparisons of DNA sequences give more reliable evidence of relationships than comparisons of appearance.
items.answer: Similar appearance may result from convergent evolution; DNA differences accumulate at a roughly constant rate, so numbers of differences reflect time since divergence; data are quantitative.
items.markingKey: convergence [1]; molecular clock / quantitative [1] [2]

items.stem: Part of the DNA sequence of a gene in species A is GACTCTATGAGCGCCCACGTAGCACACTTT. The same region in three other species is: species B: GACTCTAAGAGCGCCCACGTAGCACACTTT; species C: GACGTTAGGTGCGCCCACGGAGCAAACCTT; species D: GACTCTCTGTGAGTCCACGTAGGTAAGTTT. Use your answers to state which species is most closely related to species A. Explain your answer.
items.answer: Species B: fewest differences, so most recent common ancestor (mutations have had least time to accumulate).

items.stem: Explain how new species arise by allopatric and by sympatric speciation, and how molecular evidence can be used to show relationships between species.
items.answer: Species definition; allopatric: barrier, no gene flow, different selection/mutation/drift, reproductive isolation; sympatric: same area, behavioural/ecological/temporal isolation, polyploidy in plants; molecular: DNA/protein sequences, differences accumulate over time, fewer differences = more closely related, molecular clock, mtDNA.
items.markingKey: definition of species [1]; allopatric [2]; sympatric with example [2]; molecular evidence [2] [7]

items.stem: Which statistical test compares the means of two samples of continuous data?
items.answer: The t-test
items.markingKey: χ² is for categorical data.

items.stem: Zara says: "Discontinuous variation is always caused by the environment." Explain whether Zara is correct.
items.answer: Discontinuous variation is usually genetic, controlled by one or a few genes with little environmental influence.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Discontinuous variation is usually genetic, controlled by one or a few genes with little environmental influence. [2]

items.stem: Kwame measured the number of stomata in a field of view of leaves from the top of a tree (sample A, n = 12) and leaves from the bottom of a tree (sample B, n = 12). Sample A: mean 26.17, standard deviation 2.552. Sample B: mean 22.5, standard deviation 3.03. Explain why a t-test, rather than a chi-squared test, is appropriate for these data.
items.answer: The data are continuous measurements (approximately normally distributed) and two means are being compared; χ² is for counts in categories.
items.markingKey: The data are continuous measurements (approximately normally distributed) and two means are being compared [1]; χ² is for counts in categories [1] [2]

items.stem: Lucas measured the shell length of dog whelks on a sheltered shore (sample A, n = 10) and dog whelks on an exposed shore (sample B, n = 15). Sample A: mean 28.8 mm, standard deviation 2.394. Sample B: mean 26.6, standard deviation 0.986. (a) State a null hypothesis for this investigation. (b) Explain why a t-test, rather than a chi-squared test, is appropriate for these data.
items.answer: (a) There is no significant difference between the mean shell length of the two samples. (b) The data are continuous measurements (approximately normally distributed) and two means are being compared; χ² is for counts in categories.
items.markingKey: (a) There is no significant difference between the mean shell length of the two samples [1] (b) The data are continuous measurements (approximately normally distributed) and two means are being compared [1]; χ² is for counts in categories [1] [2]

items.stem: Ines measured the height or mass of individuals in a clone of strawberry plants in Seoul and found that the data formed a normal distribution. (a) Describe how you would decide whether the mean value differs significantly from that of a second population. (b) Explain the difference between variation caused by genes and variation caused by the environment in terms of whether it can be inherited.
items.answer: (a) Measure a large random sample from each; calculate means and standard deviations; carry out a t-test with df = n₁ + n₂ − 2; compare t with the critical value at p = 0.05. (b) Genetic variation is passed to offspring in gametes; environmental variation is not inherited (it changes the phenotype, not the alleles).
items.markingKey: (a) random samples [1]; t-test [1]; compare with critical value [1] [3] (b) Genetic variation is passed to offspring in gametes [1]; environmental variation is not inherited (it changes the phenotype, not the alleles) [1] [2]

items.stem: In the Hardy–Weinberg equation p² + 2pq + q² = 1, what does 2pq represent?
options: The frequency of the recessive allele
The frequency of the dominant allele
items.answer: The frequency of heterozygotes
items.markingKey: p² homozygous dominant, q² homozygous recessive.

items.stem: After a flood kills most of a small population at random, allele frequencies change. What is this an example of?
items.answer: Genetic drift (a bottleneck)
items.markingKey: Random change, not selection.

items.stem: Grace says: "Natural selection produces the mutations that an organism needs." Explain whether Grace is correct.
items.answer: Mutations are random; selection acts on existing variation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Mutations are random; selection acts on existing variation. [2]

items.stem: On a beach with black and white pebbles, both very dark and very pale snails survive bird predation better than intermediate-coloured snails. Identify the type of selection and explain how it changes the population.
items.answer: Disruptive selection: extreme colours are camouflaged on one pebble type each; intermediates are seen and eaten.
items.markingKey: type [1]; explanation in terms of survival, reproduction and allele frequency [2] [3]

items.stem: Aisha is studying a recessive dark wing colour among moths in a city park. About 1 in 10,000 moths show the condition, which is caused by a homozygous recessive genotype. Calculate the frequency of the recessive allele, q.

A population of 30 lizards was carried to a new island in Cape Town's region by a storm. After 30 generations, the frequency of an allele for striped skin was 0.69, compared with 0.11 on the mainland. (a) Explain how the founder effect could account for this difference. (b) State why the Hardy–Weinberg principle would not apply to the island population.
items.answer: (a) The founders were a small, random sample of the mainland population, which by chance had a high frequency of the striped allele; the new population started with different allele frequencies and less genetic variation. (b) The population is small (drift) and there may be selection, so allele frequencies are not constant.
items.markingKey: (a) small sample [1]; by chance not representative [1]; reduced variation [1] [3] (b) The population is small (drift) and there may be selection, so allele frequencies are not constant [1]

items.stem: State why inbreeding of crop plants can reduce yields.
items.answer: Increased homozygosity exposes harmful recessive alleles, reducing vigour (inbreeding depression).
items.markingKey: Increased homozygosity exposes harmful recessive alleles, reducing vigour (inbreeding depression) [1]

items.stem: Arjun writes in a revision note: "Selective breeding creates new alleles for the desired characteristic." Identify the error and write a correct statement.
items.answer: Selective breeding increases the frequency of existing alleles; new alleles arise only by mutation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Selective breeding increases the frequency of existing alleles; new alleles arise only by mutation. [2]

items.stem: Records from a breeding programme in Mumbai show that the mean grain yield of maize rose from 2.2 t ha⁻¹ in 1960 to 8.7 t ha⁻¹ in 2020. Suggest two reasons, other than selective breeding, for the increase.
items.answer: Better nutrition / feed or fertiliser; irrigation; pesticides / veterinary care; improved management and machinery.
items.markingKey: any 2 from: Better nutrition / feed or fertiliser; irrigation; pesticides / veterinary care; improved management and machinery (1 mark each) [2]

items.stem: Records from a breeding programme in Lima show that the mean annual milk yield of dairy cows rose from 4200 kg in 1960 to 8080 kg in 2020. (a) Calculate the percentage increase. (b) Calculate the mean rate of increase per year.
items.answer: (a) 92% (b) 65 kg per year

items.stem: Plant breeders in Santiago want to produce a new variety of wheat with resistance to rust fungus and short stems. (a) Outline how they could use selective breeding to do this. (b) Explain why breeders keep collections of wild relatives and traditional varieties in seed banks.
items.answer: (a) Identify varieties (including wild relatives / landraces) with each trait; cross them; grow offspring and select those with both traits; self or backcross and select over many generations until true-breeding. (b) They contain alleles (genetic diversity) lost from modern varieties, such as disease resistance, that can be bred into crops in future.
items.markingKey: (a) sources of alleles [1]; cross [1]; select offspring [1]; repeat over generations [1] [4] (b) source of alleles [1]; future breeding / resistance [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how mitochondrial DNA has been used to study human evolution.
items.answer: mtDNA is inherited only from the mother and does not recombine; it mutates relatively quickly; comparing sequences shows relationships and dates divergence; supports African origin of modern humans.
items.markingKey: maternal inheritance / no recombination [1]; mutation rate [1]; conclusion [1] [3]

items.stem: A student in Dubai states: "Sympatric speciation requires a geographical barrier." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Sympatric speciation happens in the same area, through behavioural, ecological or chromosomal isolation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Sympatric speciation happens in the same area, through behavioural, ecological or chromosomal isolation. [2]

items.stem: Part of the DNA sequence of a gene in the grey wolf is ACTGCTTACGAGAAATCA. The same region in three other species is: the coyote: CCTGCTTACGAGAAATCA; the red fox: ACTGATTAAGAGAAATCA; the domestic dog: ATGATGTACCAGAGCTCA. Suggest why scientists compare long sequences rather than short ones like this.
items.answer: A short sequence gives few differences, so chance has a large effect; longer sequences give more reliable estimates of relatedness.
items.markingKey: A short sequence gives few differences, so chance has a large effect [1]; longer sequences give more reliable estimates of relatedness [1] [2]

items.stem: Two populations of a ground beetle on either side of a mountain range near Mumbai were found to differ in body colour and in the timing of their breeding seasons. When brought together in the laboratory they mated but produced few fertile offspring. (a) Explain how the two populations could have become different. (b) Describe how DNA sequencing could be used to investigate how long ago the populations separated. (c) Name the type of isolating mechanism shown by the different breeding seasons.
items.answer: (a) The mountains are a geographical barrier preventing gene flow; different selection pressures (climate, predators) on each side; different mutations and genetic drift; allele frequencies diverged. (b) Sequence the same gene(s) (e.g. mtDNA) in both; count differences; use a molecular clock (known mutation rate) to estimate time since divergence. (c) Temporal (seasonal) isolation — a prezygotic mechanism.
items.markingKey: (a) barrier / no gene flow [1]; selection [1]; mutation / drift [1] [3] (b) sequence same genes [1]; count differences [1]; molecular clock [1] [3] (c) Temporal (seasonal) isolation — a prezygotic mechanism [1]
